At a trailing P/E of 9.05× against the Energy sector median of 8–14×, and EV/EBITDA of 5.83× (sector median 5–8× for capital-intensive energy firms), COALINDIA screens as fairly valued to mildly cheap on earnings multiples — though its P/B at 2.36× is at P100 (priciest) among energy peers vs a sector median of 1.6×, which is a caution signal; the forward P/E of 7.98× below trailing suggests modest earnings recovery is priced in, and the 28.1% ROE partially justifies the P/B premium. The sector card prescribes EV/sales plus unit-economics trajectory (not P/E) for pre-profit platforms: even on that basis, at forward P/E 94.94× (P99 vs 472 peers), P/B 17.98× (P95), and still-negative unit economics, the stock grades expensive — the IPO valuation already prices in a profitability ramp that is not yet visible in filings. The single biggest fundamental risk is the ~₹20,717 cr combined income-tax demand (AY 2022–24) raised by authorities, equivalent to roughly 26% of current market cap, which, if sustained on appeal, would dwarf the IPO proceeds and threaten solvency.

fundamental.thesis: CESC is a vertically integrated regulated electric utility primarily serving West Bengal through 40+ subsidiaries and joint ventures, recently expanded to Chandigarh via the ₹871 cr CPDL acquisition — it operates as a regulated-distribution annuity (judge on regulatory-period terms and commissioning pace) rather than a merchant-power name. Q1 FY26 revenue grew +7.0% YoY to ₹5,202 cr, decelerating from +10.2% in 9M FY25, while PAT of ₹387 cr (+2.4% YoY) barely moved despite a 73.5% EBITDA surge — ₹304 cr in finance costs and heavy dependence on ₹228 cr of non-recurring regulatory income (vs only ₹280 cr core operating profit, a 1.2× coverage ratio) are suppressing PAT margin to 7.3% and masking weak underlying earnings quality. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive regulated utility, 10.92× sits comfortably within the utility range and trailing P/E of 14.7× is mid-band vs the 10–18× sector median — grading fair on absolute terms; the forward P/E of 11.9× signals priced-in modest earnings growth, and peer-relative rank is cheap (P14 broadly) though this largely reflects a structural utility-sector discount rather than clear mispricing. The biggest risk is that headline EBITDA growth overstates cash earnings quality — reported PAT is structurally reliant on non-recurring regulatory income contested via APTEL appeals, layered on extreme leverage (D/E 164×) and sustained downward EPS revisions (~−8% over both 30 and 90 days) that contradict the overwhelmingly bullish sell-side stance — a classic pre-derating signal.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Teleservices (Maharashtra) is a residual B2B/enterprise-focused telecom entity serving Maharashtra and Goa, stripped of its consumer mobile business (transferred to Airtel in 2017) — it categorically does not participate in the ARPU-recovery or 2G-to-5G upgrade thesis that drives BHARTIARTL; its addressable market is narrow and structurally shrinking. FY26 revenue fell 11.3% YoY to ₹1,160 cr (a sharp reversal from +9% in FY25), and the apparent PAT improvement from -₹1,275 cr to -₹215 cr is entirely attributable to a one-time ₹666.70 cr AGR settlement credit — the underlying operational loss before exceptional items was ₹870 cr, and Q3FY26 PAT margin was -51.1%, confirming the 'expanding PAT margin' trajectory signal is illusory. At EV/EBITDA of 51.6× (vs the sector card's 9–12× yardstick for India mobile and a broad-market median of 22.6×), TTML is grossly expensive — a Price/Book of -0.44× reflects technical insolvency (negative net worth of ₹19,983 cr), making conventional valuation metrics almost meaningless, and the P90 broad-market EV/EBITDA rank confirms the market is pricing in speculative optionality, not earnings power. The primary risk is a terminal-decline feedback loop: revenue is contracting at double-digit rates with no guidance, no organic path to PAT positivity, and a debt-laden balance sheet where liabilities far exceed assets — any shortfall in AGR staggered payments or further revenue erosion could accelerate a restructuring event.

Max Financial Services (MFSL) is the listed holding company for Axis Max Life Insurance (AMLI), one of India's leading private life insurers with ₹185,827cr in total insurance assets and Axis Bank as a growing 19% strategic co-owner following multiple equity tranches. FY26 revenue decelerated sharply to +2.6% YoY (₹47,674cr, down from +7.6–8.2% at the 9M stage) while PAT attributable to owners crashed 74.3% YoY to ₹84cr (PAT margin: 0.2%), the collapse driven almost entirely by a ₹7,500cr swing in policyholders' investment fair value (₹4,721cr gain in FY25 → ₹2,779cr loss in FY26); operating cash flow at ₹11,473cr is robust, but the absence of VNB margin and APE growth data — the correct KPIs for a life insurer under the sector card's P/EV yardstick — makes true business quality assessment impossible from available filings. Every available proxy points unambiguously expensive: forward P/E 102.3× (+122% above 4-peer median of 46×), P/B 20.3× (+196% above peer median 6.8×), with MFSL ranked P100 (most expensive) across all multiples versus peers despite a depressed ROE of 1.6% — using P/EV is the correct approach per sector doctrine, but with EV absent, no angle makes valuation look attractive. The biggest risk is a recurrence of equity-market-driven MTM losses on policyholders' investments while the proposed MFSL-AMLI amalgamation awaits regulatory approvals, layering corporate-action overhang onto an already expensive, guidance-free holdco structure with a pending unprovisioned SEBI enforcement action.

fundamental.thesis: Mankind Pharma is India's #1 pharma company by prescription volume (15.1% prescription share) with a dominant domestic branded-formulations franchise (~85% revenue), chronic-segment leadership in cardiac and anti-diabetes, and significant consumer-healthcare OTC depth — a textbook India-facing 'safe template' with no direct US tariff exposure. fundamental.thesis: Bharat Forge is a global forging-to-advanced-engineering conglomerate transforming from auto-heavy revenues into defense, aerospace, and EV drivetrains, operating India's highest-margin standalone forging operation (27.5% standalone EBITDA margin in Q4FY26) while absorbing severely underperforming EU (4% EBITDA margin) and US (3.5% EBITDA margin) subsidiaries undergoing painful restructuring through CY27. FY26 consolidated revenue grew +11% YoY to ₹16,812 cr, but standalone revenue declined 5% YoY to ₹8,396 cr driven by North America CV market weakness and regulatory uncertainty, with consolidated PAT margin compressed to ~4.45% — the defense and aerospace pivot (order book ₹11,000 cr, ₹4,814 cr new business wins in Q4 alone) is visible in order inflows but not yet meaningfully in reported earnings, with revenue accretion guided from H2FY27 onward. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive forging business, the stock trades at 33.4x (P80 vs the 5-peer auto-parts median of 19.1x, a 75% premium), and at 86x trailing P/E (P100 in sector, +120% vs peer median 39.2x), near its 52-week high at 88.2% of range — the valuation is clearly expensive and prices near-perfect execution of the defense/aerospace re-rating thesis well ahead of its financial manifestation. The single biggest risk is that EU/US restructuring drag extends into FY27 (CDP liquidation only completes end-CY27, US CV cycle still soft), while any delay in converting the ₹11,000 cr defense order book to revenue at 86x trailing P/E leaves virtually no margin of safety for a business currently earning only 4.45% PAT margins at the consolidated level.

fundamental.thesis: Oberoi Realty is a premium-to-ultra-luxury residential and commercial developer concentrated in the MMR (Mumbai Metropolitan Region), operating a lumpy possession-based revenue model supplemented by growing rental annuity income — the sector card's primary valuation yardstick is EV/EBITDA (not P/E, which is structurally misleading for developers). FY26 full-year revenue grew +15.2% YoY to ₹6,304 cr with PAT up +12.7% to ₹2,508 cr, but this acceleration from H1FY26's near-flat +4.2% revenue and +0.6% PAT growth and Q3FY26's +7.0%/+0.8% reflects a heavily Q4-concentrated possession cycle rather than a broad-based demand inflection — EBITDA margins are exceptional at ~58% and PAT margins near 40%, but trajectory signals show mild contraction. EV/EBITDA of 17.54× sits below the Real Estate sector range of 20–35×, and peer rank at P34 on EV/EBITDA confirms fair-to-slightly-cheap relative pricing; however, sell-side EPS estimates have been revised down -3.0% over 90 days and the mean analyst target implies only +2.9% upside — a classic pre-derating pattern despite a still-bullish rating mix. The single biggest risk is the combination of very high reported debt/equity (15.77), negative estimate revision momentum, and the absence of any full-year or recent bookings (pre-sales) data — the one metric that actually leads real estate earnings — making it impossible to confirm whether FY26 revenue acceleration reflects genuine demand strength or a one-off completion bundle.

fundamental.thesis: AIIL is a listed NBFC and investment holding company whose economic engine is a ₹15,473 cr investment portfolio (up 21.4% YoY), with a secondary direct-lending book of ₹2,008 cr — it behaves more like a closed-end investment fund than a traditional lender, meaning revenues are structurally volatile as they capture realised/unrealised investment gains. Q3 FY26 revenue fell 22.5% YoY to ₹478 cr (a multi-quarter deteriorating trajectory from −10.8% in Q3 FY25 to −22.5% now), while PAT collapsed 70.1% YoY to ₹161 cr with PAT margin compressing sharply to 33.7% from 87.4% — the full-year FY26 picture shows revenue down 43% and PAT down 56%, though the underlying portfolio is growing, suggesting the income line reflects lower realised gains, not portfolio erosion. Using the appropriate yardstick for an NBFC/lender — P/B vs ROE — AIIL trades at P/B 2.91× against a TTM ROE of 13.1%, which is FAIR (below the P/B > 3 with ROE < 12% 'expensive' zone but well above the P/B < 1.5 'cheap' floor); the trailing P/E of 8.95× looks deeply cheap vs the NBFC sector median of 18–28× but is unreliable here given the company's volatile investment-income earnings base. The dominant risk is extreme financial leverage — D/E of 24.59× with subordinated liabilities surging 70× to ₹2,122 cr from the ₹2,050 cr 15-year NCRPS issuance — which creates severe balance-sheet sensitivity to any mark-to-market drawdown in the investment book.
